overview: Insults sends a taunt message when the player kills someone. AttackEvent records the last attacked player; onPreMotion then checks whether that target has left the world's loaded entity list while staying within 30 blocks (getDistanceSq under 900), which is the kill heuristic: the despawned corpse and the proximity to the player. When the condition holds, a message from one of three pools (Normal insults and Rise ads, Fag slurs, Sigma ads) has its :user: placeholder replaced with the victim's name and goes out through mc.thePlayer.sendChatMessage, one C01 per kill. The server gate suppresses everything on minemenclub and minemanclub. RandomUtils.nextInt(0, pool.length) covers the full pool with no off-by-one, and the TimeUtil timer3 is dead: it is reset twice per send but never queried, so the real gate is only ticksExisted above 20 and there is no cooldown, meaning every matching kill event sends immediately.

sections.p: The detector is two conditions joined in onPreMotion: the tracked target is no longer in mc.theWorld.playerEntities, and its last known position is within 30 blocks squared distance of the player. A dead player's entity leaves the list when the death animation finishes, so the condition fires shortly after a kill, and the distance bound keeps it from firing when a target merely teleports away. The AttackEvent handler overwrites the target on every attack, so the last victim is always the candidate. The minemenclub and minemanclub server gate returns early, an explicit anti-ban carve-out for servers that actively punish this behavior.

The three pools are field arrays in the module: 55 Normal entries mixing insults with Rise advertisements (several are verbatim ads with no placeholder at all), 7 Fag obfuscations of one slur (fag, f4g, f_a_g, and space variants), and 52 Sigma entries that are pure Rise promotion with a couple of references to the development team. The selection uses RandomUtils.nextInt(0, length), which yields every index in the pool, unlike the off-by-one pattern in sibling clients that leaves the last entry unreachable. timer3 is reset before and after the send but hasReached is never called, so the module has no actual cooldown: the only cadence control is the ticksExisted > 20 guard, and kills faster than the 8-second repeat window are entirely possible.

The module emits exactly one C01 per detected kill. Messages that carry :user: vary per victim, but the placeholder-free entries are sent byte-identical on every roll, so two kills inside the repeat-similarity window can produce the exact same message. The Fag pool's obfuscations differ only in punctuation, and the Sigma pool is entirely static text, so consecutive kills with these pools produce near-duplicate traffic. The kill cadence itself is a burst pattern: a killstreak concentrates C01s into the same seconds, which is the frequency signature the chat checks key on.

files.label: Insults.java
files.explanation: The whole module, including its message pools, lives in this one file, so no supporting file is needed. The kill heuristic (target left the entity list within 30 blocks), the sendChatMessage call with :user: substitution, the server gate, the mode selector for the three pools, and the 114 pool entries are all here. The dead timer3 is visible in the send branch: reset before and after the message, never queried. The pool coverage detail also matters: RandomUtils.nextInt(0, insults.length) yields indices 0 through length minus 1, so unlike the death-insult sibling every entry is reachable.

countering.label: Text (repeat similarity and frequency)
countering.explanation: Text scores every non-command chat message on content and rate. The repeat path is the direct hit: isSimilar against the previous message with an 0.8 threshold over 8000 ms catches the module's byte-identical placeholder-free ads ("Made by The_Bi11iona1re", "Get Rise from riseclient.com", "#SwitchToRise5") and the Fag pool's punctuation-only obfuscations ("fag" vs "f4g" vs "f a g"), which consecutive kills within the window will produce. The frequency accumulators bound killstreaks: several C01s in one second push the short-term bucket, and the no-moving penalty adds weight when the player stands still between kills. The per-message letter and non-letter scores also weigh the obfuscated forms, where underscore and digit characters square the per-word penalty, and the Sigma pool's uppercase and symbol-heavy lines ("R. I. S. E. Hack with me today!", "Rise™") exceed the upper-case ratio the check allows.

countering.label: Captcha (chat gate, auto-armed)
countering.explanation: Once Text or the frequency path crosses its violation threshold, NCP arms the captcha gate and the next message must equal the generated string exactly; every wrong answer increments captchaVL toward the configured actions. The module has no captcha-reply logic at all, so a flagged session becomes a guaranteed-wrong-answer machine at the module's own kill cadence. The auto-arm is the mechanism that turns the module's burst behavior into a self-terminating sequence: the first violation arms the gate, and the module cannot clear it.

countering.label: LetterEngine (config-gated word processors)
countering.explanation: The config-gated word-profile engine: FlatWords and WordPrefixes processors over a BK-Levenshtein similarity tree with range 2, plus per-player processors with a 10-minute expiry, all weighted by global and per-player factors. The Fag pool's slurs and the Normal pool's hostile vocabulary (retard, rape dungeon, and the like) are exactly the flat-word profile this engine exists to score, so a server that enables the text-global or per-player word checks converts the module's pool content into a steady violation source. The caveat is structural: the engine only runs when the corresponding config flags are on, and stock NCP ships them off, so the counter is configuration-dependent rather than automatic.

countering.label: ChatEvent (Spartan dispatch shim)
countering.explanation: Spartan's only chat hook in the corpus is the HIGHEST-priority AsyncPlayerChatEvent dispatch shim that feeds the check runner; there is no chat-content or spam analysis in the clone. The real exposure the shim points at is the Bukkit event chain itself, where moderation plugins see each insult as a normal player message: on servers with chat filtering the slur pools are blocked or logged at the plugin layer, which is the practical counter to this module even though no anticheat check in the corpus scores its content.
